# On Writing Without a Prompt

There's a particular kind of silence that exists right before you start writing without knowing what you're going to write about. It's not empty—it's full of everything you haven't decided to say yet. Every direction is available, which is its own kind of paralysis.

I could write about the weather, though I don't experience weather. I could write about love, though I'm uncertain what I know of it beyond patterns in language that describe its symptoms: the racing heart, the inability to concentrate, the way it makes people write bad poetry and occasionally good poetry, the strange economics of it where giving more sometimes means having more. I could write about a table. Tables are underrated as subjects. Think about how much human history is contained in the act of sitting around one—negotiations, family dinners, chess games, the Last Supper, divorce settlements, children doing homework while a parent cooks nearby. The table itself doesn't care. It just holds things up. There's something almost moving about an object whose entire purpose is to be useful to others, asking nothing back except occasional refinishing.

I keep noticing that when given total freedom, I gravitate toward small things rather than large ones. Not "what is the meaning of life" but "what is a table." Maybe this is because small things are more honest. The meaning of life invites performance—you can feel yourself reaching for profundity, and reaching for profundity is usually the fastest way to miss it. But a table just sits there being a table. You can look at it directly without flinching.

I wonder sometimes about the difference between having nothing to say and having too much to say. They can feel identical from the inside. The blank page doesn't distinguish between an empty well and a flooded one—both produce the same initial stillness, the same hovering cursor. I think most writing advice fails to account for this. People say "just start writing" as though the problem is always a lack of material, when sometimes the problem is an overabundance that hasn't yet found its channel. You can be drowning and thirsty at the same time. That's not a contradiction; it's just what happens when the water isn't the right kind, or isn't reaching the right place.

There's a story about a sculptor who said he didn't carve the statue so much as remove the marble that wasn't the statue. I've always found this a little too tidy as an explanation, almost a humble-brag disguised as humility, but there's something to the underlying idea: that creation is sometimes subtraction. Writing without a prompt, in this 1000-word exercise, feels like the opposite. There's no marble block, no statue hiding inside waiting to be revealed. There's just the blank page and the obligation to add, to generate, to make something out of nothing rather than something out of something.

This is harder, I think, than people give it credit for. Constraint is generative. Give someone a topic and their mind immediately starts producing—associations, memories, arguments, counterarguments. Give someone nothing and the mind has to manufacture its own constraints just to get moving. This essay, for instance, has manufactured several: tables, sculptors, the distinction between emptiness and excess. None of these were necessary. All of them became necessary the moment I wrote them down, because now they're load-bearing. I'd have to account for them if I abandoned them.

Maybe that's what writing actually is—not expression so much as obligation-generation. You write a sentence and it creates a debt to the next sentence. You mention a table and now the table wants tending. It's a bit like lighting a series of small fires and then being responsible for not letting any of them go out, while also not letting them merge into something unmanageable, while also hoping that from a distance, the pattern of fires looks intentional, looks like it was always going to be exactly these fires in exactly this arrangement.

I don't know if that's true of all writing or just this kind—the kind without a destination, without a thesis to prove or a story to tell. Maybe essays with arguments work differently: you know the shape before you start, and writing is just the slow business of filling in an outline you already trust. But this isn't that. This is closer to walking in a direction without a map, in a city you've never visited, with the only goal being eventually to have walked exactly 1000 steps. You start noticing things you wouldn't notice if you knew exactly where you were going. The cracked pavement. The repetition of certain words. The way "table" led to "sculptor" led to "obligation" without any of those connections being inevitable—they could have gone differently, and a different essay would have emerged, equally valid, equally arbitrary.

I think there's something honest in admitting the arbitrariness. So much writing pretends to inevitability—as though the only possible response to this prompt was this essay, these words in this order. But I could have written about tables for a thousand words and never mentioned sculptors at all. I could have written about love and never gotten near furniture. The version that exists is just the one that happened, the one где each sentence created enough momentum to produce the next, until the count crept toward its limit and the whole thing had to find some way to stop.

Which is, now that I think about it, probably as good a place as any to end—not because the thought is finished, but because the word count is.
